source_text: Si ergo contendunt hoc competisse novitati, ut quemadmodum non ex viri semine, ita nec ex virginis carne caro fieret dei verbum, quare non hoc sit tota novitas, ut caro non ex semine nata carne processerit? Accedam adhuc cominius ad congressum. Ecce, inquit, virgo concipiet in utero. Quidnam? utique dei verbum, non viri semen, certe ut pareret filium. Nam et pariet, inquit, filium. Ergo ut ipsius fuit concepisse, ita ipsius est quod peperit, licet non ipsius fuerit quod concepit. Contra si verbum ex se caro factum est, iam ipsum se concepit et peperit, et vacat prophetia. Non enim virgo concepit neque peperit, si non quiequid peperit ex verbo concepto caro ipsius est. Sola haec autem prophetae vox evacuabitur? an et angeli conceptum et partum virginis annuntiantis? an et omnis iam scriptura, quaecunque matrem pronuntiat Christi? Quomodo enim mater, nisi quia iu utero eius fuit? Sed nihil ex utero eius accepit quod matrem eam faceret in cuius utero fuit. Hoc nomen non debet caro extranea. Matris uterum non appellat nisi filia uteri caro. Filia uteri porro non est si sibi nata est. Tacebit igitur et Elisabeth prophetam portans iam domini sui conscium infantem, et insuper spiritu sancta adimpleta. Sine causa enim dicit, Et unde mihi ut mater domini mei ad me veniat? Si Maria non filium, sed hospitem in utero gestabat Iesum, quomodo dicit, Benedictus fructus uteri tui? Quis hic fructas uteri, qui non ex utero germinavit, qui non in utero radicem egit, qui non eius est cuius est uterus et qui utique fructus uteri, Christus? An quia ipse est fles de virga profecta ex radice Iesse, radix autem Iesse genus David, virga ex radice Maria ex David, flos ex virga filius Mariae, qui dicitur Iesus Christus, ipse erit et fructus? Flos enim fructus, quia per florem et ex flore omnis fructus eruditur in fructum. Quid ergo? Negant et fructui suum florem et flori suam virgam et virgae suam radicem, quominus suam radix sibi vindicet per virgam proprietatem eius quod ex virga est, floris et fructus; siquidem omnis gradus generis ab ultimo ad principalem recensetur, ut iam nunc carnem Christi, non tantum Mariae, sed et David per Mariam et Iesse per David sciant adhaerere. Ideo hunc fructum ex lumbis David, id est ex posteritate carnis eius, iurat illi deus consessurum in throno ipsius. Si ex lumbis David, quanto magis ex lumbis Mariae, ob quam in lumbis David?
thought_title: The Virgin's flesh must be Christ's own flesh
orientation: Tertullian is arguing against those who say the Word became flesh without taking flesh from the Virgin's womb, and he now presses the testimony of Isaiah and Elizabeth to show that Mary was truly Christ's mother.
pass_a_gloss: If therefore they contend that this suited the newness, that just as not from the seed of a man, so also not from the flesh of the virgin the Word of God should become flesh, why should this not be the whole newness, that flesh not born from seed should come forth from flesh? I will approach still more closely to the contest. Behold, he says, a virgin shall conceive in the womb. What indeed? certainly the Word of God, not the seed of a man, certainly so that she should bear a son. For she shall also bear, he says, a son. Therefore just as it was hers to have conceived, so it is hers what she bore, although it was not hers what she conceived. On the contrary, if the Word from itself was made flesh, then it itself conceived itself and bore itself, and the prophecy is void. For the virgin did not conceive nor bear, if whatever she bore is not his flesh from the Word conceived. But will this voice of the prophet alone be made void? or also the angel's announcing the conception and birth of the virgin? or also all the Scripture now, whatever proclaims the mother of Christ? For how is she mother, except because it was in her womb? But it received nothing from her womb that would make her mother in whose womb it was. This name flesh foreign to her does not owe. It does not call her the mother's womb unless the flesh is daughter of the womb. But daughter of the womb it is not if it was born to itself. Therefore Elizabeth also will be silent, carrying the prophet already aware of his Lord, the infant, and moreover filled with the Holy Spirit. For without cause she says, And whence to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? If Mary was carrying in her womb not a son but a guest, Jesus, how does she say, Blessed is the fruit of your womb? What is this fruit of the womb, which did not sprout from the womb, which did not put down root in the womb, which is not of her whose the womb is, and which certainly is the fruit of the womb, Christ? Or because he himself is the flower from the branch sprung from the root of Jesse, and the root of Jesse is the family of David, the branch from the root is Mary from David, the flower from the branch is the son of Mary, who is called Jesus Christ, will he himself also be the fruit? For the flower is the fruit, because through the flower and from the flower every fruit is trained into fruit. What then? Do they deny to the fruit its flower and to the flower its branch and to the branch its root, so that the root may not claim for itself through the branch the property of that which is from the branch, of the flower and of the fruit; since indeed every step of descent from the last to the first is recounted, so that now they may know that the flesh of Christ adheres not only to Mary, but also to David through Mary and to Jesse through David. Therefore this fruit from the loins of David, that is from the posterity of his flesh, God swears to him will sit upon his throne. If from the loins of David, how much more from the loins of Mary, on account of whom he is in the loins of David?

pass_b_english: So if they insist that this was fitting for the newness of the thing—that just as the Word did not become flesh from a man's seed, so neither did he become flesh from the virgin's flesh—why should the whole newness not be this: that flesh not born from seed came forth from flesh? I will come still closer to the contest. “Behold,” he says, “the virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isaiah 7:14). What shall she conceive? The Word, certainly, not a man's seed—and certainly so that she might bear a son. For “she shall bear,” he says, “a son.” Therefore, just as it was hers to conceive, so what she bore is hers, even though what she conceived was not hers. On the other hand, if the Word became flesh from himself, then he conceived and bore himself, and the prophecy is void. For the virgin did not conceive and did not bear, if whatever she bore from the Word she conceived is not his flesh. But will only this voice of the prophet be made void? Or also the angel's announcement of the virgin's conception and birth? Or also all Scripture now, whatever proclaims the mother of Christ? For how is she his mother, unless because he was in her womb? But he received nothing from her womb that would make her a mother in whose womb he was. Flesh that is foreign does not deserve this name. No one calls it a mother's womb unless the flesh is a daughter of the womb. But it is not a daughter of the womb if it was born from itself. So Elizabeth too will be silent—she who was carrying the prophet, an infant already aware of his Lord, and who was moreover filled with the Holy Spirit. For she says without cause, “And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). If Mary was carrying in her womb not a son but a guest, Jesus, how does Elizabeth say, “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42)? What is this fruit of the womb, which did not sprout from the womb, which did not put down root in the womb, which does not belong to the one whose womb it is—and which is certainly the fruit of the womb, Christ? Or is it because he himself is the flower from the branch that came forth from the root of Jesse, and the root of Jesse is the family of David, the branch from the root is Mary from David, the flower from the branch is the son of Mary, who is called Jesus Christ—will he himself also be the fruit? For the flower is the fruit, because through the flower and from the flower every fruit is brought to ripeness into fruit. What then? Do they deny to the fruit its flower, and to the flower its branch, and to the branch its root, so that the root may not claim for itself through the branch the ownership of what is from the branch—the flower and the fruit? Since every step of descent is traced from the last back to the first, let them now know that the flesh of Christ clings not only to Mary, but to David through Mary, and to Jesse through David. Therefore God swears to him that this fruit from the loins of David—that is, from the posterity of his flesh—will sit on his throne (Psalm 132:11). If from the loins of David, how much more from the loins of Mary, through whom he was in the loins of David?

problems.quote: Therefore, just as the conceiving was hers, so what she bore is hers, even if what she conceived was not hers.
problems.source_quote: Ergo ut ipsius fuit concepisse, ita ipsius est quod peperit, licet non ipsius fuerit quod concepit.
problems.why: The Latin says the Word (ipsius) is the one who conceives and whose child it is; the English reverses agency to the virgin.
problems.fix: Therefore, as it was the Word’s to conceive, so it is the Word’s that she bore, even if what she conceived was not his.
problems.ruling: Latin 'ipsius' refers to the virgin throughout: her conceiving, her bearing, though what she conceived (Word) wasn't hers.

problems.quote: that flesh not born from seed came forth as flesh
problems.source_quote: ut caro non ex semine nata carne processerit
problems.why: carne is source: flesh not born of seed still came forth from flesh.
problems.fix: that flesh not born from seed came forth from flesh
problems.ruling: 'Carne' is ablative of source: flesh not born of seed 'came forth from flesh' (the virgin's). 'As flesh' drops that and loses the argument.

problems.quote: He does not call a mother's womb his own unless the flesh is a daughter of the womb.
problems.source_quote: Matris uterum non appellat nisi filia uteri caro.
problems.why: No male subject and no “his own”; a womb is a mother’s womb only as flesh born of it.
problems.fix: No one calls it a mother's womb unless the flesh is a daughter of the womb.
problems.ruling: Subject of 'appellat' is 'caro'. The English adds a male 'He' and 'his own', so it misattributes who names the womb.

problems.quote: how does she say, “Blessed is the fruit of your womb”
problems.source_quote: quomodo dicit, Benedictus fructus uteri tui
problems.why: dicit continues Elizabeth, who blesses Mary; the English makes Mary the speaker.
problems.fix: how does Elizabeth say, “Blessed is the fruit of your womb”
problems.ruling: 'Dicit' is Elizabeth, but 'she' right after 'Si Maria...' reads as Mary. The reader is misled about the speaker, so name Elizabeth.
